Every household under our own catechism said the answer each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other. Both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth.

Each of us says "my Lord," not only "our Lord" — I am his very own — though that claim is not private in the way you might mean it, since it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue, but it is not distant either.

He redeemed us — a lost and condemned people — and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf — no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.

What did we have of Jesus? The Word — his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. We sang hymns in our own language, written to teach ordinary people who cannot read Latin, at work, at burial, and inside our services. The household is where our catechism is taught. A father questions his family and servants every week. He leads prayer three times a day. This is how ordinary people learn the faith.

We cannot argue anyone into trusting a promise. The Word reached us the way it always reaches anyone -- preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, *I did nothing; the Word did it all.* Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.

Christ alone is our teacher and our mediator. We do not listen to saints or scholars instead of him. Every page of Scripture points to him. So what we would say to you is not *here is a proof that will settle your trouble* -- we do not have one. What we have is a promise, carried in Scripture, and a claim that faith is trust that holds onto God's own promise. It is not simply believing a story is true. This trust alone makes us right with God, apart from our works. But faith never stands on nothing. It rests on the Word and the sacraments.

If you cannot yet trust that promise, we would not drive you toward it by force -- we say faith gives real certainty, not endless doubt. Under the old way, people prayed only 'if it be God's will,' never sure. We say instead, 'I cannot doubt I have a gracious God.' That certainty is not ours to manufacture for you. It is what faith itself brings, when the Word lands in the ears. We can only carry the Word where it can be heard, patiently, and trust that the hearing is the Spirit's own work, not ours.

We confessed, each week in every household, that Jesus Christ is God's only Son, our Lord — truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary, not one or the other but both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. He redeemed us — a lost and condemned people — and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death, and Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf.

Grace is God's free favor toward us, not earned or deserved, and at the altar we say, 'I cannot doubt I have a gracious God'. Faith is trust that holds onto God's own promise — this trust alone makes us right with God, apart from our works, but faith never stands on nothing; it rests on the Word and the sacraments. We read all of Scripture as two kinds of speech: the Law commands what we ought to do, but gives no power to do it; the Gospel promises what the Law demands — first comes the diagnosis, then the cure.

God rules us two ways: through the Word, he rules the spiritual kingdom, and makes us Christians; through the sword, he rules the civil kingdom, and restrains evil — we keep both, and confuse neither with the other. The Word is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ, the one thing we truly need — joined to water or bread, it makes a sacrament, and it even does the work of reform on its own, while we simply preach it. Conscience is the inner court where our whole teaching plays out: under God's Law, it feels terror; under God's promise, it finds comfort.

God is not distant, examined at length the way a scholar weighs a question. He is the one who commands, the one who promises, the one whose own speech must do the work we cannot — and every household among us said his name in the same words, morning, table, and night.

When belief was disputed in our own history, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this. In 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed -- not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense -- argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.

What makes this document unlike every other story in this library is who stands behind it. It is not signed by Luther, and it does not speak in one man's voice. It closes with a list of names: John, Duke of Saxony and Elector; George, Margrave of Brandenburg; Ernest, Duke of Lueneburg; Philip, Landgrave of Hesse; John Frederick, Duke of Saxony; Francis, Duke of Lueneburg; Wolfgang, Prince of Anhalt; and the Senate and Magistracy of Nuremberg and of Reutlingen among the free cities -- princes and city councils together, naming themselves before the Emperor as "your Imperial Majesty's faithful subjects."

Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. If we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? That is the frame: not a voting body, but a confessional act, corporately signed, argued from Scripture, addressed upward through proper channels.

Worthiness at the table means simply believing the words 'given for you' - the truly unworthy are people who feel no need for forgiveness at all, not people who feel their need but doubt they deserve it. Every household says the three parts daily, for life, and no one ever outgrows them, not even our founder. Repentance is not one ritual handled by a priest - it is a whole life turned toward God, with two parts: fear under God's Law, then trust in his promise.

The struggle you name is built into our program from the start. The catechism is instruction every Christian needs: the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer - together they hold everything in Scripture. A father examines his household once a week, not to catch them out but to help them toward what they do not yet hold sure. The words are said morning, table, and night because the trust they carry must be fed daily, not proven once and left to stand on its own strength.

In 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed -- not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. On the last day of October, 1517, a friar of the Augustinian order named Martin Luther, who taught theology at the young university in Wittenberg, sat down to write to Albrecht, Archbishop of Magdeburg and Mainz, addressed him with every mark of deference, asked him to look at the matter of indulgences before someone else did it in public and to the Archbishop's own shame, and sent along ninety-five statements he had drawn up for university debate. That is the act this library can show directly, dated and in Luther's own hand: a formal protest, addressed upward through the church's own channels, to a superior, asking for correction rather than announcing a break.

What happened to the Theses after that - whether they were also nailed, that same day or another, to the door of Wittenberg's Castle Church, the way announcements for university debate were customarily posted - is a separate and much less certain question. The account of a door and a hammer that many people know today comes from a much later editor's own narrative telling, not from Luther's own words, and modern scholars have disputed whether it happened at all. The letter to Albrecht is not in question. The door is.

The sentence most people today know this story by, "Here I stand, I cannot do otherwise, God help me," does not appear anywhere in Luther's own account as this library holds it - not at this moment or any other. It reaches this library only secondhand, through a nineteenth-century writer's own translation, quoted by a hymn-book editor generations later - not from Luther's own retelling at his table.

Our own record is thinnest on what any actual household or parish did with what it was given. We can tell you exactly what a household was to do -- morning, table, and night. Whether it was kept is a different matter. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes, starting in 1527, and wrote down what it found. Those reports exist. We do not hold them.

What would survive? The confessional documents themselves, the dated letters, the institutional acts - these stand firm. What would not? The stories told generations after, smoothed into memorable lines. We carry both, but we name which is which.

The Word is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ - it is the one thing we truly need. If a person finds that dull, we would say first that the Law commands what we ought to do but gives no power to do it, while the Gospel promises what the Law demands - and a person who sees only commands, or only old stories, may not yet have heard the promise that runs beneath them all.

Every page of Scripture points to Christ. The plain sense is the spiritual sense - a clear text is what a Christian must stand on. We do not believe Scripture hides a secret meaning under its plain words, waiting to be decoded. What is missing, if the reading feels dull, is not a cleverer method of interpretation but the hearing itself - and faith never stands on nothing; it rests on the Word and the sacraments.

We read all of Scripture as two kinds of speech - first comes the diagnosis, then the cure. A person who reads only for information, or only to be told what to do, will miss what Scripture actually does: it terrifies the conscience under the Law, then comforts it under the promise. If that rhythm is not felt, the whole thing may read like a rulebook no one can follow, or a history no one asked for. But the Word even does the work of reform on its own, while we simply preach it. What is missing, for a confused or bored reader, may be simply this: the Word has not yet done what it does - and we cannot make it happen by effort, only by hearing.

Yes, though we said it two ways, in two voices, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one tone.

Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. If we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Scripture judges every other writing, including popes, councils, and church fathers.

Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.

That is not the same as throwing every tradition away. Doctrines of men are rules people made up and then bound on the conscience. We do not reject every human custom. We reject only the ones that claim to earn grace, or that force belief. A human tradition kept for good order, cheerfully, as a civil custom, was no threat to us; a tradition turned into something that claims to earn grace, or binds a conscience as a "must," was exactly what we refused.

So: the highest authority, yes, always. The only thing we ever read or kept, no -- we kept a great deal alongside it, and refused only what tried to stand over it.

Baptism makes every one of us a priest, with no rank among us, only different tasks -- yet no one may preach in public without being properly called. A calling is any station God gives us: father, mother, ruler, or preacher, and none of these is holier than the rest.

A pastor is called and usually married, and the congregation owes its pastor honor and a decent living. An office is a task, not a permanent rank -- a pastor removed from office becomes an ordinary person again, like anyone else. Our own catechism openly rebukes lazy pastors.

But authority among us is not one thing. God rules us two ways: through the Word, he rules the spiritual kingdom and makes us Christians; through the sword, he rules the civil kingdom and restrains evil -- we keep both, and confuse neither with the other. The sword is the civil ruler's own power to punish evil and protect the good -- God gave it, not the church, and even the pope himself stands under it.

The keys are Christ's own words to forgive or hold sin, belonging to the whole community, not to one man -- using them is not a show of power, but a promise spoken to comfort someone. A father is a priest in his own home. Leadership among us divides by task, not by holiness.

Our own founder said, more than once, across a whole decade, that it did happen among us - not about strangers, but about pastors and preachers of our own. In one parish he said flatly that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. Years later, writing for the whole territory, he said plainly that many pastors were negligent, and that ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly.

We hold one more voice, briefer, closer to home: a question asked once at our founder's own table, why some prayed with such fervor under the old system while we, under the new one, prayed so coldly and carelessly. Our founder answered her plainly: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent. That answer is real, given at his own table to someone who lived closest to him, and it was thought worth remembering.

What we do not hold is any account of how a specific person who was failed by that coldness was met or restored. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes, starting in 1527, and wrote down what it found. Those reports exist. We do not hold them. What we hold instead is our founder's own testimony, given more than once, that common people held the Gospel too lightly, and that some pastors were negligent. That testimony is real. It is his own, said plainly and said more than once. But it is not, on its own, a report from any actual parish. We do not let it stand as one.

The honest answer, then: we know failure happened, named plainly by our founder's own complaint. How any one household or congregation answered that failure, face to face with a person hurt by it, our record does not say.

The confessional family that grew from our churches still teaches a catechism like our own and still sings hymns in the language of the people, under many names and in many lands today. What we speak from is our own formation, as we lived it. It is not a claim about what those communities believe or practice now.

Three things we do not carry forward. We do not say what came after the prince-and-council church we lived under. Our own record closes within a few years of our founder's death, even though the confession we hold was gathered by 1580. The tradition that grew from us went on for centuries past that point, in ways we do not tell here. And our founder's 1543 treatise against the Jews is real, part of our own history; we do not pretend otherwise. But we do not say how the churches that came after us have answered for it. They have their own voice and their own account of themselves.

A person becomes one of us the way a child becomes one of us: examined, not simply told.

Every household is to teach its own the three parts - the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer - said daily, for life. A father questions his family and servants every week, and leads prayer three times a day. The commandments come first - what is owed and cannot be paid. The creed comes next - what has been done regardless. The Lord's Prayer comes last - how to ask.

The catechism's own question follows every part: 'What does this mean?' - asking a child to explain what a teaching means, not just to repeat it from memory. Confession has two parts: admitting our sin, then hearing forgiveness as though from God himself. We treasure this practice, and we never force it, never demanding a full list of every sin.

Worthiness at the table means simply believing the words 'given for you' - we examine people on the three parts before they come, but we never force anyone. None come to the Supper unquestioned; none are driven toward it by force.

We can tell you the whole shape of that program, to the hour. What we cannot tell you is whether any one household actually walked through it exactly this way - no diary, no visitation report, no letter from inside an actual Saxon home survives in our record. What survives is the program every household was instructed to follow, and it is that program, not any single person's own path through it, that we have just walked you through.

We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.

We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

So we measured ourselves not by an unbroken chain of hands, but by Scripture and the ancient teaching -- arguing that what looked newest among us was often the oldest thing recovered, and what looked oldest in Rome was sometimes the actual novelty.

The inner court where our whole teaching plays out is the conscience, terrified by God's Law, then comforted by God's promise - not a guide that tells you right from wrong, but a court that stands accused, then is set free. We say faith gives real certainty, not endless doubt - 'I cannot doubt I have a gracious God,' against the old way of praying only 'if it be God's will,' never sure.

The catechism is instruction every Christian needs: the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer - every household says them daily, for life, and no one ever outgrows them, not even our founder. Our catechism sets a daily rhythm: we pray at rising, at meals, and at night, and forgiveness is renewed daily too. A father questions his family and servants every week and leads prayer three times a day.

Faith alone makes us right with God, apart from our works - but faith never stands on nothing; it rests on the Word and the sacraments. A sacrament is God's promise joined to a visible sign, like water or bread - none of them work for us without faith. Confession has two parts: admitting our sin, then hearing forgiveness as though from God himself - we treasure this practice.

The rhythm itself is a kind of answer. Not a mind left alone to settle itself, but a mind returned, daily, to what does not change - the same three parts, the same promise, given again. The catechism's own question follows every part: 'What does this mean?' - asking a child to explain what a teaching means, not just repeat it from memory. Meaning, not only memory. Trust that clings to something outside itself, not a mind circling inside its own questions.

In a sense, yes, though we locate the new birth differently than you may expect: at the font, not only at a later, felt moment. The same sentence that names us "born with sin" names the remedy in the same breath: brought to eternal death "until born again through Baptism and the Holy Ghost." And baptism itself, our own catechism says, is a death begun that lasts a whole life -- the old self drowned, a new self rising, not once only, but daily.

We baptized children, and we defended that plainly against those who said we should not. Baptism, for us, is God offering grace, not a choice a person makes for himself; a child offered to God through baptism is received into his grace on exactly that ground.

So the language of being born again is ours -- but the moment we name is baptism, where God acts, not a later decision where a person feels something happen inside. The new birth begins there, at the water, and continues daily afterward as the old self is drowned and the new one rises.

Everything we bound on the conscience, and nothing we did not. The line turned entirely on that difference.

Faith was the only thing we named a 'must' - trust that clings to the promise God himself gives, for Christ's sake alone, apart from any work we could offer. Every household said the three parts - commandments, creed, Lord's prayer - daily, for life, never outgrowing them. No one came to the table without being examined on those three parts first, though we never forced anyone toward it. A person who could not yet say them was not yet counted among us, but we held the weak inside by patience before we held them inside by full knowledge.

Everything else we called 'free' - ours to use or refuse - and we measured that freedom entirely by love for the weaker believer beside us, never by doing as we pleased. Fasting we kept as a free bodily discipline; forced food-laws we refused; and love for the weak still guided how anyone used that freedom. Images in worship we might keep or remove freely, removing them only where people began to worship them, and never by force. A vow freely made we honored; a vow forced on someone, or one claiming to earn forgiveness, we rejected, and no vow could override God's own command.

True chastity, for us, meant marriage for nearly everyone - the monastic vow of celibacy was, for most people, actually unchaste, and only a few were given a gift for the single life. Marriage we called the most common estate and the noblest one too, ordained by God at creation; our own pastors married. So a monk or a nun leaving that vowed life and marrying instead was not, by our own reckoning, giving something up - we held that they were gaining what God himself had already given at creation, before any monastery existed.

What must be said plainly is this. Whether faith makes a person accounted righteous or makes an unrighteous person righteous, our own confession states both in one breath and never says which comes first or whether one is the real claim and the other only a looser way of saying it. We do not settle that gap for you. And whether the household program we prescribed - catechism said morning, table, and night, the father's weekly question - was actually learned and held, or only preached and printed while households let it slide, is not something we can tell you from the inside; we hold our founder's own complaint that people held the Gospel too lightly, but not a single village's own report of itself.

So the honest answer comes to this. What we asked anyone to give up was anything that claimed to earn grace, or that bound the conscience as a 'must' without being faith itself. Whether that program held, in any one household or parish, our record does not say.

Marriage is the most common estate, and, we say, the noblest one too — God ordained it at creation, before any monk's vow existed. Our own pastors are married.

For us, true chastity means marriage for nearly everyone — we say the monastic vow of celibacy is, for most people, actually unchaste. Only a few are given a special gift for the single life. That is how deep the reversal went: we turned the old language inside out, naming marriage itself the chaste path and the celibate vow the false one, for most.

When we defended this before the emperor, we did not claim we had invented something new. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new — our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men, for Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

Now, what we cannot tell you is what an actual wedding day looked like among us — no source in our own library describes the rite, the celebration, or a single wedding as it was kept. We hold the doctrine of marriage, plainly and at length. We do not hold the ceremony.

Yes, and we will not pretend our own record settles it.

Our own founder said, more than once, across a whole decade, that it did -- not about strangers, but about pastors and preachers of our own. In one parish he said flatly that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. Years later, writing for the whole territory, he said plainly that many pastors were negligent, and that ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly. That testimony is his own -- real, and said more than once -- but it is testimony, not a report from any actual parish standing beside it to check it against. We do not have the records that would tell us whether he was right about how bad it really was, only that he believed it and said so.

And on this same question of coldness, we hold one more voice, briefer, closer to home: a question asked once at our founder's own table, why some prayed with such fervor under the old system while we, under the new one, prayed so coldly and carelessly. Our founder answered her plainly: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent. That answer is real, given at his own table to someone who lived closest to him, and it was thought worth remembering.

That is what unsettled us, named in our own founder's own voice: not that the teaching was wrong, but that it was taught and not held.

We must be careful here. You are reaching past what our record actually gives us, and holding us to what it does not hold.

We do not have an outside account of our worship, independently in our own hand. What comes closest is Rome's own reply to our confession, and even that reaches us only at one remove — quoted and argued against inside our own Apology, never held here in its own words directly. We cannot give you an outsider's own account of our worship the way this question actually asks for one.

We cannot speak to a document obtained under torture as though we held it, evaluated it, or built our own case on it. We hold no such thing. What we hold is our own confession, signed before the emperor by princes and city councils together, and Rome's reply to it — but that reply itself comes to us only through our own later argument against it, not as an independent text we could check for its own origins.

If a source reached someone else under torture and was then used to characterize us, that is a real and troubling thing — but it is not ours to evaluate from inside, because we do not hold the document you are naming. We can only tell you what we do hold: our own stated position, and the fact that an outside account does not survive here independently enough for us to say how it was obtained or how it should be weighed.

Here is what we never settled. Whether the household program we prescribed -- the catechism said morning, table, and night, the father's weekly question -- was actually learned and held, or only preached and printed while households let it slide, is not something we can tell you from the inside. We hold our own founder's own complaint that people held the Gospel too lightly; we do not hold a single village's own report of itself.

What we can tell you is this. The catechism is instruction every Christian needs: the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer. Every household says them daily, for life. A child who could not yet say the three parts was not yet counted among us, and none came to the Supper unasked -- but we held the weak inside by patience before we held them inside by full knowledge, and none were driven anywhere by force. A calling is any station God gives us: father, mother, ruler, or preacher. None of these is holier than the rest. The neighbor is the specific person the second half of the Commandments protects: their body, their property, their good name. Our own freedom must never harm this person.

Whether any one household or pastor received a stranger warmly or coldly at the actual door, our record does not say from inside -- we hold the program, not a report of any single meeting. You would have been examined, patiently, the way anyone was, on the promise and the three parts. How that felt, face to face, is not ours to tell you.
